title: The Second Opinion

post.author: u/saltcote_foreman_delyth
post.title: I'm foreman of the jury for a coastal poetry prize. This year's winner passed our copy checker. On Thursday a letter arrived with the same poem, printed in 1927.

blocks.text: The Saltcote Prize has run on our stretch of coast since 1979; this is its 48th year, and about 2,400 poems come in each autumn. I've been foreman of the jury for six of them. Since 2021 every entry goes through a copy checker before we read it. A volunteer developer built it: it searches an archive of 40,000 published poems with hybrid search, a keyword score (BM25, which counts the words two texts share) and an embedding, merged into one ranking by a rule called reciprocal rank fusion. The top 5 go to a language model, which reads the entry beside them and answers copied or not copied.

2026-10-01 22:14  entry 2026-0417 "Lamp Oil"  top 5 retrieved
2026-10-01 22:14  judge: NOT COPIED

On Saturday 3 October we gave the prize to "Lamp Oil" by Ambrin Verrall. Six stanzas, a lighthouse lamp-room, a woman keeping a light nobody visits. On Thursday a letter came from a librarian in Wexmoor, with a photocopy of "The Lamp-Room" by Rhosyn Peverell, from the winter 1927 number of *The Wexmoor Quarterly*. Every line of "Lamp Oil" is reworded, a close paraphrase. The images are the same, in the same order, in the same stanzas. Only the first stanza is new: the sea at night.

1927  I keep the light that no one comes to see.
2026  I tend a flame that nobody will visit.
Rhosyn Peverell was lost from the Wexmoor ferry one January night in 1931. She has been dead ninety-five years, and this month she won our prize.

On Friday our developer reran the entry and showed me the archive's 12 closest poems. Eleven are about the sea. He also tried a different kind of model, one that reads two texts side by side and scores whether they say the same thing; he called it a cross-encoder. It gave "The Lamp-Room" 0.91. Nothing else scored above 0.31.

diagram.aria: The rerun of entry 0417. Top row, the fused ranks 1 to 3: Night Ferry, 1994, 0.03252; The Harbour at Two, 2003, 0.03227; Low Tide, Lamps Lit, 1981, 0.03175. Middle row: Fishermen's Chapel, 1968, 0.03126, 4th; Salt Wind, 2011, 0.03101, 5th; The Lamp-Room, 1927, 0.02904, 7th, BM25 12th and vector 6th, not sent. Bottom: the checker's verdict, NOT COPIED, from the five sent; and the cross-encoder, which gave The Lamp-Room 0.91 and nothing else above 0.31.

notes.text: Rerun, Friday 9 October: hybrid search, fused score

blocks.caption: Drawn from Friday's rerun. Hybrid search's top 5 by fused score, all sea poems: Night Ferry 0.03252, The Harbour at Two 0.03227, Low Tide, Lamps Lit 0.03175, Fishermen's Chapel 0.03126, Salt Wind 0.03101. The Keeper's Wife, 1975, came 6th at 0.03008 (not drawn). The Lamp-Room came 7th at 0.02904: last of the 12 by BM25, 6th by the embedding. Only the top 5 went to the judge.

blocks.text: Ambrin Verrall says she wrote it in one night on the harbour wall and had never heard of Rhosyn Peverell. The committee has asked me what we change before entries open again in January. What do I change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in that archive is haunted. Your checker has two kinds of reader in it, and only one is switched on. The embedding model is a bi-encoder: it turns each poem into one vector on its own, long before it meets the entry, and the search compares vectors afterwards. One vector holds the whole poem, sea stanza included. The model your developer tried is a cross-encoder: it reads the entry and one poem together, as a single input, and gives the pair one score. A candidate is a poem the search hands on for a closer look, and to rerank is to score candidates again with a more careful model and reorder them. Three questions. Where did The Lamp-Room come in each list? How long did the cross-encoder take? And do you have entries you already know were copied, to test against?

replies.author: u/saltcote_foreman_delyth
replies.text: BM25 put it last of the 12: a score of 4.1, against 14.2 for Night Ferry, because hardly a word is shared. The embedding put it 6th, at 0.78. Merged, 7th. The cross-encoder took 72 ms for the 12 pairs, 6 ms a pair on the office's one graphics card. As for known copies: five entries we caught by hand in earlier years, and this week the jury wrote seven more as tests. Our developer ran all 12 known copies through the checker as it stands. It caught 4.

comments.author: u/fifty_is_fine_lisette
comments.text: The model is smart enough; just give it 50. Five was the whole mistake: your poem came 7th. Send the top 50 and let the model read every one, the way a careful juror would, and it will see the match on the first pass. Models read hundreds of pages at a time now. Fifty poems is nothing.

replies.author: u/saltcote_foreman_delyth
replies.text: Our bill is 0.2 cents a call plus 0.1 cent for each poem the model reads. Fifty would be 5.2 cents an entry instead of 0.7.

replies.author: u/fifty_is_fine_lisette
replies.text: Five cents not to crown a ghost. Cheap at the price.

comments.author: u/back_numbers_dilys
comments.text: I sent the letter. *The Wexmoor Quarterly* printed The Lamp-Room in its winter number of 1927; I know of three copies, and our library holds one. Rhosyn Peverell was the Wexmoor Point keeper's daughter. What I can't put down is the new first stanza. Ms Verrall's sea at night is the winter crossing to Wexmoor: the pier lamps going out behind, the second bell, the cold coming up through the deck. Rhosyn never finished that crossing.

replies.author: u/saltcote_foreman_delyth
replies.text: Ambrin Verrall told me on the phone that she has never been to Wexmoor.

reply.prompt: Entries open again in January. What should the Saltcote checker do before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Send the top 50 straight to the model: it is smart enough to read them all and spot the poem that was copied.
options.verdict: In the prompt, not in the answer
options.part2: The committee had the checker send the top 50 straight to the judge. Our developer reran Lamp Oil first. The Lamp-Room went in this time, 7th of 50, with sea poems on every side, and the judge said NOT COPIED. On the 12 known copies it caught the same 4 as before, the ones whose sources came 1st, 1st, 2nd and 3rd; a source in 41st place sat in the middle too. Each entry now takes 3.55 s and costs 5.2 cents instead of 0.7: $124.80 a year for the same four catches. The poem was in front of the model. It just didn't use it.
options.senior: More poems in the prompt is not more attention. Models tend to use what sits at the start and end of a long input better than what sits in the middle (lost in the middle), and 49 other poems are noise around the one that matters. Send few, and make sure the right one is among them: that is the job of a careful second ranking, not of the judge.

options.text: Retrieve 100 by hybrid search, rerank them with the cross-encoder, send the top 5, and test on known copies.
options.part2: We kept hybrid search but took its top 100, had the cross-encoder score all 100 pairs with the entry, and sent the top 5 of its order to the judge. Lamp Oil first: The Lamp-Room rose from 7th to 1st at 0.91, far ahead of The Keeper's Wife at 0.31, and the judge said COPIED. Then the 12 known copies: 11 caught. The one missed had its source outside the top 100, where no reranker could see it. Each entry takes 1.90 s instead of 1.30 s, 600 ms of it for 100 pairs at 6 ms each. The judge still reads 5 poems, so the bill stays 0.7 cents an entry, $16.80 a year. The known copies now run before every change to the checker.
options.senior: Two stages: a fast, wide first stage for recall (hybrid search, 100 candidates) and a slow, careful second stage for precision (a cross-encoder on 100 pairs), so the model reads only the 5 that matter. Measure both: is the source in the 100, and is it in the 5? The rerank costs time in proportion to the candidates, so choose k from the test, not by feel.

options.text: Switch to a bigger embedding model and embed all 40,000 poems again, so close paraphrases climb into the top 5.
options.verdict: One place closer, still not sent
options.part2: We switched to a bigger embedding model and re-embedded all 40,000 poems over a weekend. Lamp Oil again: The Lamp-Room rose from 6th to 4th in the vector list, and from 7th to 6th merged. The top 5 were still sea poems, and the judge said NOT COPIED. On the known copies it caught 5 of 12, one more than before. The new model still gives each poem one vector, made before it meets the entry, and the new sea stanza still pulls the entry toward every sea poem in the archive.
options.senior: A better bi-encoder moves ranks a little; it can't compare two texts line by line, because it never sees them together. Keep it for the first stage, where speed over 40,000 poems matters, and do the line-by-line comparison where it is affordable: on a short list.

options.text: Have the model compare each entry with every one of the 40,000 poems, one call each, so that nothing is missed.
options.part2: We had the judge read Lamp Oil against every poem in the archive, one call each. It found The Lamp-Room, and on the known copies it caught 12 of 12, the only setting that ever did. But each entry took 40,000 calls: 11 h 40 min and $120.00. For 2,400 entries that is $288,000.00 a year, and the jury reads in March.
options.senior: Comparing an entry with everything, using the most careful reader, is exact search done with a model: perfect recall, and a cost that grows with every poem you add. Put the careful reader on a short list instead: a cheap first stage finds 100, the careful reader checks those. Keep the full comparison, if at all, for a spot check after the winner is chosen.

sim.title: Rerun the Saltcote checker yourself
sim.lede: You're Delyth on Friday, rerunning the winning entry, Lamp Oil. There is no real model and no real embedding. The sim holds a teaching sample of 12 of the archive's 40,000 poems, each with a stated BM25 score, a stated cosine similarity to the entry (from the current embedding model and from a bigger one), and a stated cross-encoder score for the pair. Its BM25 rank and vector rank are its places among the 12; as a teaching assumption, the other 39,988 poems rank below all 12 in both lists. Hybrid search merges the two lists by reciprocal rank fusion: each list adds 1 divided by (60 + the poem's rank), and the poems are sorted by the sum, the fused score. Candidates from 13th to 100th are unnamed filler that the cross-encoder scores 0.02 each (the prize's log says none of them scored higher). With the reranker on, the first k candidates, up to the number you choose to rerank, are sorted by their cross-encoder score. The top n go to a stand-in judge, which follows a stated rule in place of a model: of s poems sent, it notices a copied source in the first 5 or the last 5 places and misses one in between, a rough stand-in for lost in the middle. Times and costs are the prize's measurements: 50 ms for the first stage, 6 ms a pair for the cross-encoder, and for the judge 1.0 s plus 0.05 s a poem, 0.2 cents a call plus 0.1 cent a poem. Below the tables, the jury's 12 known copies: for each, the place hybrid search gave its source and whether the judge would catch it.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you start on the night: top 5, no reranker. The Lamp-Room is 7th at 0.02904 and isn't sent: NOT COPIED, 4 of 12 known copies caught, 1.30 s and 0.7 cents an entry. Pick Send the top 50 straight: it goes in 7th of 50, in the middle, and is still missed, 4 of 12, 3.55 s, 5.2 cents. Pick Retrieve 100, rerank, send 5: it rises to 1st at 0.91, COPIED, 11 of 12, 1.90 s, still 0.7 cents. Now set the candidates retrieved to 5 with the reranker still on: the reranker never sees it. Try reranking 50 (10 of 12, 1.60 s) and 12 (7 of 12, 1.37 s). Pick the bigger embedding model: 6th, still missed, 5 of 12. Pick the judge reading all 40,000: 12 of 12, at 11 h 40 min and $120.00 an entry.

explain.oneLine: Nothing haunted the checker. One vector per poem filed Lamp Oil, new sea stanza and all, among the sea poems, so The Lamp-Room came 7th and only 5 were sent. A cross-encoder, reading each pair together, put it 1st at 0.91.

steps.title: One vector per poem: a bi-encoder.
steps.text: The checker's embedding model turns every poem into one vector on its own, and the search compares vectors afterwards by cosine similarity. That is why it is fast: the 40,000 vectors were made once, ahead of time, and an entry needs only its own. But one vector has to hold the whole poem, and Lamp Oil's new opening stanza about the sea at night pulls it toward every sea poem in the archive. The Lamp-Room came 6th by the embedding and last of the 12 by BM25, because every line was reworded. Merged, it came 7th, and only the top 5 were sent.

steps.title: Reading the pair together: a cross-encoder.
steps.text: A cross-encoder reads both texts as one input and gives the pair one score. Nogueira and Cho's passage reranker, built on BERT, feeds the query as sentence A and the passage as sentence B, outputs the probability that the passage is relevant, computes it for each passage independently, and ranks by it. Because it sees both texts at once, it can notice that every line of one matches a line of the other. The price: nothing can be computed ahead of time. It runs once per pair, at query time: 6 ms a pair on the prize's graphics card.

steps.title: Retrieve many, rerank to a few.
steps.text: So you split the work. The first stage is cheap and wide: hybrid search takes the top 100, and the question is recall at 100, whether the source is anywhere in the list. The second stage is careful and narrow: the cross-encoder scores those 100 pairs and the top 5 go on, and the question is precision at 5, whether the five sent are the ones worth reading. In the sim, retrieving 100 and reranking puts The Lamp-Room 1st and catches 11 of the 12 known copies.

steps.title: Why not send 50 straight to the model.
steps.text: Two reasons. Cost: the judge is paid by the poem it reads, so 50 poems cost 5.2 cents an entry against 0.7 and take 3.55 s against 1.30 s. And attention: models tend to use the start and end of a long input better than the middle (lost in the middle, Season 1). In the sim, The Lamp-Room arrives 7th of 50 and the stand-in judge misses it; the known copies stay at 4 of 12.

steps.title: The rerank costs time in proportion to the candidates.
steps.text: At 6 ms a pair, reranking 12 candidates adds 72 ms, 50 add 300 ms, 100 add 600 ms, and 1,000 would add 6 s. Choose the number from the known copies, not by feel: in the sim, reranking 12 catches 7 of 12 at 1.37 s an entry, 50 catch 10 at 1.60 s, and 100 catch 11 at 1.90 s. The 12th copy's source isn't in the top 100 at all; more reranking can't reach it.

diagram.aria: The fix. The entry goes to hybrid search over 40,000 poems, 50 ms, which hands its top 100 to the cross-encoder: 100 pairs at 6 ms each, 600 ms. The top 5 go to the judge model, 1.25 s and 0.7 cents, which returns the verdict COPIED, The Lamp-Room at 0.91. The 12 known copies are run before every change: 11 of 12 caught.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for January. Hybrid search stays as the first stage but hands on 100 candidates; the cross-encoder reads each one with the entry, 100 pairs at 6 ms, 600 ms; the judge reads only the top 5. Lamp Oil comes back COPIED, The Lamp-Room 1st at 0.91, in 1.90 s and 0.7 cents. The 12 known copies run before every change: 11 caught.

fix.title: The fix: retrieve 100, rerank with a cross-encoder, send 5, and test
fix.text: Keep hybrid search as the first stage and raise what it hands on from 5 to 100 candidates. Score each of the 100 against the entry with a cross-encoder trained to judge whether two texts say the same thing, and send the top 5 of its order to the judge. Lamp Oil comes back COPIED, The Lamp-Room 1st at 0.91, in 1.90 s an entry, and the judge's bill stays at 0.7 cents because it still reads 5 poems. Then keep the known copies as a test set: run all of them after any change to the search, the reranker or the numbers, and track two things separately: is the source in the top 100 (recall at 100), and does it reach the 5 sent? Today that is 11 of 12.

limits: A reranker can only reorder what the first stage hands it. The 12th known copy's source isn't in the top 100, so no reranker sees it; that miss has to be fixed in the first stage, for example by searching with each stanza separately or by rewriting the query (case 7 of this season).

The time grows with every candidate: 600 ms for 100 pairs here, 6 s for 1,000. A hosted rerank API adds a network call and a bill per search, and long texts get cut: Cohere's reference says long documents are truncated to max_tokens_per_doc, 4,096 tokens by default.

A cross-encoder's score says how alike two texts are, not whether one was copied. A model trained on paraphrases may miss a translation or a loose imitation, and two poems can match on a shared source both drew on. The jury still decides.

explain.seniorTake: Retrieval is two jobs with opposite needs. Finding candidates in a big collection needs speed, so you use representations made ahead of time: BM25 and one vector per document. Putting the right few on top needs care, so you use a model that reads the query and each candidate together, and you can only afford it on a short list. Decide three numbers on purpose: how many to retrieve (for recall), how many to rerank (for time), and how many to send (for cost and attention). Then measure them on cases where you already know the right answer, because neither the first stage nor the model will tell you what it missed.

realWorld.title: Nogueira and Cho, 2019: BERT as a reranker
realWorld.text: Rodrigo Nogueira and Kyunghyun Cho's Passage Re-ranking with BERT (arXiv 1901.04085, first posted January 2019) describes a simple re-implementation of BERT for query-based passage re-ranking. In their method, they feed the query as sentence A and the passage text as sentence B, truncate the query to at most 64 tokens and the whole input to 512, obtain the probability of the passage being relevant, compute this probability for each passage independently, and obtain the final list by ranking with respect to these probabilities. The abstract reports the state of the art on TREC-CAR and the top entry on the MS MARCO passage leaderboard, outperforming the previous state of the art by 27% (relative) in MRR@10.

realWorld.title: Nogueira and Cho: retrieve a thousand first
realWorld.text: The same paper frames the reranker as a second stage: a large number (for example, a thousand) of possibly relevant documents is first retrieved by a standard mechanism, such as BM25, and the model reranks those. Its MS MARCO evaluation pairs each query with the top 1,000 passages retrieved with BM25. The paper reports no inference time; the only timing it gives is training, about 30 hours on a TPU v3-8.

realWorld.title: Sentence Transformers: bi-encoder against cross-encoder
realWorld.text: The Sentence Transformers documentation says Bi-Encoders produce for a given sentence a sentence embedding, while a Cross-Encoder does not produce a sentence embedding: we pass both sentences simultaneously to the Transformer network. It says Cross-Encoder achieve better performances than Bi-Encoders, however, they do not scale well for large datasets. Its example: clustering 10,000 sentences with Cross-Encoders would mean scoring about 50 million sentence combinations, which takes about 65 hours; with a Bi-Encoder, computing an embedding for each sentence takes only 5 seconds.

realWorld.title: Sentence Transformers: retrieve and re-rank
realWorld.text: The same page recommends combining them: first, you use an efficient Bi-Encoder to retrieve e.g. the top-100 most similar sentences for a query; then, you use a Cross-Encoder to re-rank these 100 hits by computing the score for every (query, hit) combination. That is the shape of the Saltcote fix, with hybrid search as the first stage.

realWorld.title: Sentence Transformers: speed falls as models grow
realWorld.text: The library's pretrained cross-encoder table lists MS MARCO models with a Docs/Sec column: cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 at 1,800, ms-marco-MiniLM-L12-v2 at 960 and ms-marco-electra-base at 340, with MRR@10 of 39.01, 39.02 and 36.41. The page doesn't say what hardware measured them, so treat them as relative speeds. For paraphrase-style pairs it lists Quora duplicate-question models that give a score 0…1 indicating the probability that two questions are duplicate questions. The prize's 6 ms a pair is its own measurement.

realWorld.title: Cohere: a hosted rerank API
realWorld.text: Cohere's Rerank endpoint, its reference says, takes in a query and a list of texts and produces an ordered array with each text assigned a relevance score. It recommends against sending more than 1,000 documents in a single request, top_n limits the number of returned rerank results, and max_tokens_per_doc defaults to 4,096, with long documents automatically truncated.

realWorld.title: Cohere: the models on offer
realWorld.text: Cohere's overview says Rerank indexes the documents from most to least semantically relevant to the query, and lists rerank-v4.0-pro, rerank-v4.0-fast, rerank-v3.5, rerank-english-v3.0 and rerank-multilingual-v3.0; it describes Rerank 4.0 and 3.5 as multilingual, which matters when an entry and its source are in different languages.

realWorld.title: An LLM as the reranker
realWorld.text: A language model can also do the reranking. Sun and colleagues' Is ChatGPT Good at Search? (arXiv 2304.09542, 2023) investigated generative LLMs such as ChatGPT and GPT-4 for relevance ranking and found that properly instructed LLMs can deliver competitive, even superior results; a distilled 440M model outperformed a 3B supervised model on the BEIR benchmark. It usually costs more and takes longer per candidate than a small cross-encoder.

realWorld.title: Liu and colleagues: lost in the middle
realWorld.text: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (arXiv 2307.03172, 2023) found that performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context, and degrades when it is in the middle. The sim's stand-in judge is a rough rule built on that finding, not a measurement of any model.

realWorld.title: Reciprocal rank fusion, k = 60
realWorld.text: Elasticsearch's reference describes reciprocal rank fusion as a method for combining multiple result sets with different relevance indicators into a single result set, adding 1.0 / (k + rank) for each result set a document appears in. Its ranking constant, rank_constant, defaults to 60, the value the sim uses.

asked: What is a reranker, and when is it worth the latency?
Bi-encoder or cross-encoder: what is the difference?
How many documents should you retrieve, and how many should you send to the model?
interview.answer: A bi-encoder embeds each text on its own, so document vectors can be computed ahead of time and searched in milliseconds; a cross-encoder reads the query and one document together and scores the pair, which is more accurate but has to run once per pair at query time. So a reranker is a second stage: a cheap first stage, BM25, vectors or both, retrieves a wide list for recall, say 50 to 100, and the cross-encoder reorders it so the few you send are the right ones. It is worth the latency when the right document is often retrieved but not near the top, which you find out by measuring recall at the wide k and at the small n on a test set with known answers. Its cost grows with the candidates, a few milliseconds a pair on a GPU, so pick k where recall stops improving. Send only a handful to the model: each extra document costs tokens and money, and models tend to use the middle of a long input worst. And remember the limit: a reranker can only reorder what the first stage found.

terms.def: The member of a judging panel who chairs it and speaks for it. Delyth chairs the Saltcote Prize jury.
A group of lines in a poem, set apart like a paragraph. Lamp Oil has six stanzas; The Lamp-Room has five.
The glass room at the top of a lighthouse where the lamp burns.
Here, the lighthouse keeper: the person who tends a lighthouse and its lamp.
A magazine published four times a year.
The same meaning said in different words. Lamp Oil rewords every line of The Lamp-Room.
The Saltcote Prize's program that checks each entry against the archive before the jury reads it, and answers copied or not copied.
The prize's collection of 40,000 published poems, typed up so the checker can search them.
A keyword-search score: a text scores higher the more of the query's words it contains, especially rare words. It counts shared words, not meaning.
Running keyword search (BM25) and vector search for the same query and merging the two ranked lists into one.
Merging several ranked lists into one ranking.
Rank fusion where each list adds 1 / (k + rank) to a document's score, with k usually 60, and the merged list is sorted by the sums.
A poem's RRF score in the checker: 1 / (60 + its BM25 rank) + 1 / (60 + its vector rank). The Lamp-Room's is 0.02904.
A model that encodes each text alone into one vector; texts are compared afterwards, by cosine similarity. Vectors can be made ahead of time, so search is fast.
A model that reads two texts together as one input and outputs one score for the pair. Usually more accurate than comparing vectors, but it must run for every pair at query time.
Here, the entry and one candidate poem, scored together by the cross-encoder.
A document the first stage hands on for a closer look.
The fast, wide search that picks candidates from the whole collection: here, hybrid search over 40,000 poems.
The slower, careful scoring of the first stage's candidates: here, the cross-encoder.
To score the first stage's candidates again with a more careful model and reorder them by the new scores. The model that does it is the reranker.
The language model call that reads the entry and the poems sent and answers copied or not copied.
The sim's rule in place of a model: of s poems sent, it notices a copied source in the first 5 or last 5 places and misses one in between.
Entries the jury knows are copied, with their sources marked, used to test the checker: 5 caught by hand in earlier years and 7 written as tests.
Here, the share of known copies whose source is among the first k candidates. Recall at 100 asks: did the first stage find it at all?
The share of the first k results that are relevant. Precision at 5 asks: are the 5 sent the ones worth reading?
How long a request takes, from sending it to having the answer. Here, the time to check one entry.
A millisecond, a thousandth of a second.
A chip built for many small calculations at once. Models such as a cross-encoder run much faster on one than on an ordinary processor.
A simplification the sim states openly so its numbers stay exact, such as the other 39,988 poems ranking below all 12 in both lists.
In the sim, the unnamed candidates from 13th to 100th, each scored 0.02 by the cross-encoder.
Compute new embeddings for every stored item, needed whenever you change embedding model.
A provider's service that takes a query and a list of texts and returns them reordered with relevance scores, so you don't run the model yourself.
A company that sells language models through an API, including rerank models.
Cohere Rerank settings: top_n limits how many reordered results come back; max_tokens_per_doc cuts each document to that many tokens (4,096 by default).
Cut a text off at a maximum length.
A transformer language model Google released in 2018, often fine-tuned to classify or score text.
BERT's two input slots, separated by a marker token, so it can read two texts as one input.
A large public dataset of real search queries and passages, used to train and test passage rankers.
A research dataset for retrieving Wikipedia passages, from the Complex Answer Retrieval track of TREC, a long-running search evaluation conference.
Mean reciprocal rank in the top 10: 1 divided by the rank of the first right answer, 0 if none is in the top 10, averaged over queries.
Google's own chip for training and running neural networks, comparable to a GPU.
Documents per second: how many query and document pairs a model scores each second.
An open-source Python library for embedding models (bi-encoders) and cross-encoders.
A family of small, fast transformer models; L6 and L12 in a model name give its number of layers.
A large language model used to put candidates in order of relevance. Often accurate, but slower and costlier per candidate than a small cross-encoder.
A public collection of retrieval benchmarks across many kinds of text.
A small model trained to copy a bigger model's outputs.
A widely used open-source search engine that supports keyword search, vector search and their fusion.
Elasticsearch's name for the k in reciprocal rank fusion. It defaults to 60.
A question-and-answer website. Its public set of question pairs marked duplicate or not is used to train paraphrase models.
OpenAI's chat assistant and one of the language models behind it.
A model trained on examples labelled with the right answer, here query and passage pairs marked relevant or not.
Model sizes in parameters: 440 million and 3 billion.
Sending many pairs through a model in one go, which uses a GPU better than one pair at a time.
Changing or splitting a search query before searching, so it matches the way the right documents are written.
A search box that shows results while the user is still typing, so each search must return in a few hundred milliseconds or less.
A page in a company's help centre that explains one task or problem to customers.
A chat assistant that answers customers' questions, here from help articles.
Working across many languages. A multilingual embedding or reranker can match a text with its translation.
An international standard for quality management systems. A company can be audited and certified against it.
ISO 9001:2015 clause 7.1.5: when you use a check to verify products or services, you provide what is needed for valid, reliable results.

atWork: Find an assistant at work that searches before it answers: a support assistant, a handbook bot, an internal search. A common incident: the right help article is retrieved but ranked eighth, the top 5 are sent, and customers get an answer about something nearby. Sending more is the usual first idea; it raises the cost per question and pushes the right article into the middle of a long prompt. Instead, retrieve a wider list, such as the top 50, rerank it with a cross-encoder you host or a hosted rerank API, and send the top 5 of the new order. Measure the time it adds: at 6 ms a pair, a figure you should measure on your own hardware, 50 pairs add about 300 ms a question, which is often acceptable for a chat answer and often too much for search-as-you-type. Build a test set of questions whose right articles the owners have marked, and track two numbers separately: is the right article in the top 50, and does it reach the 5 sent. Standards-readiness note: if your company holds or is pursuing ISO 9001:2015 certification and the assistant's answers form part of the service you deliver, clause 7.1.5 (monitoring and measuring resources) asks that checks used to verify a product or service give valid and reliable results; a retrieval test set with known answers, run before each change and kept as a record, is that evidence, so build it in now rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your company's support assistant answers from 6,000 help articles: vector search takes the top 5 and sends them to a model. For the question about moving an account to a new phone, the right article comes back 8th and is never sent; the five sent are about new phones in general. A teammate wants to send the top 20 instead. What do you tell them, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Sending 20 straight puts the right article in the middle of a long prompt, where models use it worst, and costs more per question
Retrieve a wider list and rerank it with a cross-encoder that reads the question and each article together, then send the top few
Measure it on a test set with known right articles: is the article in the wide list, does it reach the few sent, and how much time is added

recall.model: I'd tell them the article was found, just not near the top, and that sending 20 straight puts it in the middle of a long prompt, where models tend to use information worst, while every question costs more and the model reads more noise. I'd keep the vector search as the first stage but take a wider list, say the top 50, and rerank it with a cross-encoder that reads the question and each article together, then send the top 5 of its order. Then I'd measure it: a test set of questions with known right articles, checking recall at 50 (is the article in the list) and whether it reaches the 5 sent, plus the latency the rerank adds, a few milliseconds per pair.

recall.prompt: What is the difference between a bi-encoder and a cross-encoder?
options: A bi-encoder handles two languages; a cross-encoder handles one language at a time.
A cross-encoder makes better vectors, so it is used to build the search index ahead of time.
A bi-encoder turns each text into a vector on its own and compares vectors afterwards; a cross-encoder reads both texts together and scores the pair.
They are the same model; a cross-encoder simply returns a bigger top-k.
recall.why: A bi-encoder encodes each text alone, so a collection's vectors can be made ahead of time and searched fast. A cross-encoder produces no vector at all: it reads the query and one document as one input and outputs one score, which is more accurate but must run for every pair at query time. That is why it is used as a reranker on a short list.

recall.prompt: A cross-encoder takes 6 ms a pair on your hardware. You retrieve 300 candidates and rerank all of them for every query. How much time does the rerank add to each query?
options: 6 ms, because the pairs are scored together in one call
recall.why: The rerank runs once per pair, so its time grows with the candidates: 300 pairs at 6 ms each is 1,800 ms, 1.8 seconds. Batching on a GPU can cut it, but the work still grows with the candidate count. Measure recall on a test set to see whether 300 buys anything over 50 or 100.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: how many documents should a RAG system retrieve, and how many should it pass to the model? Explain how you would choose.

keyIdeas.idea: Retrieve a wide list (tens to a hundred or so) so the right document is in it: the first stage is judged on recall
Pass only a handful to the model, after reranking, for precision, cost and because models use the middle of long inputs worst
Choose both numbers by measuring on a test set with known answers, within a latency and cost budget

recall.model: I'd split it into two numbers. Retrieve wide, tens to a hundred or so candidates, because the first stage is judged on recall: the right document has to be somewhere in the list, and nothing later can recover it if it isn't. Then rerank with a cross-encoder and pass only a handful, around the top 5, to the model: that's precision, it keeps the cost per request down, and models tend to use the middle of a long input worst, so a long list can hide the right document even when it's there. I'd choose both by measuring on a test set with known answers: recall at the wide k and whether the answer reaches the top 5, against a latency budget, since the rerank costs a few milliseconds per candidate.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The checker now retrieves 100, reranks them with the cross-encoder and sends 5. The known copies have grown to 20, and it catches 19. In March the jury found a copy by hand anyway: the winner of our new Welsh-language section turned out to be an English poem from 1952, translated. The checker passed it. Our developer says the 1952 poem never came back in the top 100 at all. A committee member now wants to rerank 1,000 candidates for every entry, to be safe.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the translation get past the checker, and should every entry rerank 1,000?

keyIdeas.idea: The source never reached the reranker: BM25 shares no words across languages and an English-only embedding can't match a translation, so it wasn't retrieved
Use multilingual models for the first stage and the reranker, or translate entries before searching, and add translated copies to the known copies
Reranking 1,000 costs about 6 seconds an entry, ten times today's 600 ms, and can't help if the source isn't in the 1,000: measure recall at k on the known copies first

coldCase.model: It got past because it never reached the reranker. The first stage couldn't find it: BM25 shares no words between a Welsh entry and an English poem, and an English-only embedding doesn't place a translation near its original, so the 1952 poem wasn't retrieved and the cross-encoder never saw the pair. Fix the first stage: use multilingual models, for the embedding and the reranker, or translate each entry into English before searching, and add translated copies to the known copies so this kind of miss is tested every time. Reranking 1,000 wouldn't have helped, because the poem wasn't in the top 1,000 for the same reason, and at 6 ms a pair it costs about 6 seconds an entry, ten times today's 600 ms. Measure recall at k on the known copies first and raise k only if the sources are sitting just below 100.
